title: Three Likenesses of the One Redemption: First Man, Living Spirit, Third Ambassador
arc: The teaching poses a single question — "to what are these three likened?" — and answers with three parables that show how the First Man's descent, the Living Spirit's building-and-rescue, and the Third Ambassador's recovery are one redemptive movement seen in three discrete registers.
reading:
This chapter is built as a riddle and its three answers. The opening question — "the First Man, the Ambassador, and the abode (the ship): to what are they likened?" — is the master's way of teaching that these three names do not point to three unrelated agents but to three distinct moments of a single redemptive work. By answering with three parables, the teaching lets us see how the same divine intention enters the natural in three different modes, each corresponding to a discrete degree of operation.

The First Man is likened to a famous man whose property and sons have been taken from him, who comes down from the Height after his scattered children, into the very midst of his enemies. Read by correspondence, this is Divine Truth in its primal descent: the Lord, in his own form of love-and-wisdom, going after his own — his "two sons," explicitly identified as the Living Soul, the divine truth dispersed in the natural. The detail that he "shines forth in the Sweetness" places this descent under the quality of divine good: it is not first a war but an emanation, an outpouring of the Father's own savor reaching toward what has been scattered. This is why the two sons stand "in two powers, performing the fourth watch" — the Living Soul lives in the polarity of the mingled state and labors through the appointed station of vigil until extraction is complete. The First Man is therefore the redemptive mission as such, the original going-forth of the Divine into the realm of self-love after what is his own.

The ship and the Living Spirit are then given as a second register. The ship — the doctrinal vessel, here also the luminary-ship that carries light across the natural — is likened to a great furnace, and within that furnace dwells the Living Spirit. The image is exact: the vessel of ascent is not an empty boat but a forge, a place where heat is concentrated and material reworked, and the operative Divine power resides at its heart. The Living Spirit is then doubled in two further likenesses. He is a wise craftsman who adorns and fashions every full-armament for the war — Divine Wisdom in its shaping power, building the apparatus by which the soul fights — and he is a warrior who goes to the foot of a king's son held captive and draws him by the hand out of the enemies' grasp. Where the First Man descends as father, the Living Spirit operates as artisan and rescuer: he builds the order, supplies the armor, and reaches into the place of bondage to extract the captive prince. This is the structuring, executive aspect of the same redemption.

The Third Ambassador, though the section is much broken, is likened to a "great man" whose work is told in the same vocabulary — wealth to be recovered, the hand of captives, the powers of light, sons with their soul, a country in which the captive has been carried away. The Ambassador, in correspondence, is the awakening call, the Lord's specific operation through revealed image to extract good from the mingled state. The parable here turns toward the recovery itself: the wealth in the captors' hand, the soul taken into a foreign country. Where the First Man descends and the Living Spirit builds and pulls, the Third Ambassador summons — he is the revealing word that reaches the captive in the country of her captivity and turns her face homeward.

Read together, the three parables articulate one work in three discrete degrees. The First Man corresponds to the inmost descent of Divine Truth into the natural — the going-after as such, manifest in the Sweetness of divine good. The Living Spirit corresponds to the operative middle degree — the shaping wisdom that constructs the war-armament and the warrior-hand that draws the bound prince out of enemy hands. The Third Ambassador corresponds to the outermost reach into the captive country — the call that finds the soul where she has been carried and recovers the scattered wealth. The three are therefore not rivals or repetitions but the celestial, spiritual, and natural-rational registers of a single rescue: the Father going after his sons, the Spirit building and grasping, the Ambassador calling and recovering. The recurring images — sons taken, property scattered, captives in enemy hands, the country of captivity — are deliberately the same across all three, because the object of redemption is one (the Living Soul), while the modes by which the Lord reaches it are the discrete three the teaching names.
